issues.explanation: The trigger 'Arab villages' is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of physical abuse by a romantic partner and the rest of the profile, which centers on interpersonal abuse-related cues, self-appraisals, and memory phenomena. Without any corresponding threat, memory, or appraisal content involving war, military, or ethnic/geographic conflict, this item appears clinically incoherent for this patient.

issues.item: Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control
issues.explanation: Strictly restricting eating to feel in control is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The other selected items coherently describe PTSD related to partner physical abuse (criticism, violence, offender cues; fragmented/alien memory; rage; dehumanization, self-blame, emotional numbing; distraction and cue avoidance). In contrast, restrictive eating introduces a distinct control-focused coping pattern that is not reflected elsewhere in triggers, memory, threat, or appraisals, making it clinically hard to explain as part of the same formulation rather than a separate problem.

vignette:
Kaelani is a 74-year-old divorced editor who came to therapy at the urging of his adult daughter, after months of increasingly isolated living. The event that shattered his life happened nearly forty years ago, during his marriage to a woman he had loved deeply. The abuse was not constant, but it was devastating when it came-usually after she had been drinking, and usually triggered by something he had said or done that displeased her. He remembers one night in particular, not as a continuous story but as a series of frozen images: the way her hand looked as it swung toward his face, the crack of his head against the kitchen cabinet, the smear of blood on the white tile floor. The memory feels alien to him, as though it belongs to someone else, yet when he recalls it he is flooded with an intense, burning rage that leaves him shaking.

In the years since the divorce, Kaelani has built a careful life around avoiding anything that might remind him of her. He works from home as an editor, which allows him to control his environment, but even that has become difficult. When a client sends back a manuscript with corrections, the criticism lands like a physical blow. His heart pounds, his jaw tightens, and he feels himself becoming an object again-something to be used and discarded. In those moments, the memory of that night rushes back unbidden, the snapshot images playing in his mind like a slideshow he cannot stop. He has come to believe that the abuse happened because of the sort of person he is: weak, deserving of punishment, fundamentally flawed. This belief colors every memory he has of the marriage, making the past feel both vivid and unreal.

To cope, Kaelani has developed a set of strategies that have slowly shrunk his world. When a wave of anger or shame rises, he immediately distracts himself-turning on the television, picking up a crossword puzzle, scrolling through news articles he does not really read. He avoids any strong emotion, because he has learned that feeling too much leads to that rage, and the rage leads to the memory, and the memory confirms everything he fears about himself. He will not watch movies with conflict, will not answer the phone if he is not sure who is calling, will not visit the grocery store during busy hours. He has stopped seeing old friends, because they might ask about his life, and he would have to feel something. This avoidance has made the memory more intrusive, not less; the more he pushes it away, the more it surfaces at unexpected moments, and the more he feels like a stranger to himself.

The cycle has tightened over the years. The less he allows himself to feel, the more convinced he becomes that he will never feel normal emotions again. The more he avoids reminders of his ex-wife, the more sensitive he becomes to any perceived criticism or correction, which then triggers the memory again. He is certain that if he let himself feel the rage fully, he might do something terrible, so he stays in a state of constant vigilance, monitoring his own emotional state for any sign of danger. His work has suffered; he has lost several contracts because he could not tolerate the feedback process. His daughter has noticed that he no longer laughs, no longer argues, no longer seems present in his own life.

What finally brought Kaelani to therapy was the moment he realized he had not left his apartment in three weeks. His daughter brought him groceries, and when she asked why he looked so tired, he could not find the words to explain. He is afraid that talking about the memory will make it worse, that he will be swallowed by the rage and never find his way back. But he is also afraid of staying where he is-a man who has become a ghost in his own story, waiting for a past that will not let him go.
